$comment: What each tool is and when to use it: the introductions of the docs' Tools pages (docs/tools/…, workbench/playground/tool-docs.mjs) and the labels of their diagrams. what: a few plain sentences. when: the situations it fits, one line each. not: what it can't do, with the tool that can (optional). get: where to get it, a path on the site (tools/#… is the tools page). video: a demo in docs/videos (workbench: workbench/docs/videos). shots: gallery screenshots (docs/images/gallery, the workbench's in workbench/docs/images/gallery), by their name without -light/-dark; their captions come from the start page's gallery. In text: `code`, **bold**, [links](https://…), (@site:<path>) for a page of the site and (@docs:<slug>) for another page of the docs. groups: the Tools section's groups, in order. core: the middle of the "one engine" diagram. flow: a handler's path, the steps of the second diagram. Write it the way you'd explain it to someone on Discord (AGENTS.md, Conventions).

tools.title: Workbench
tools.what: The workbench is a handler editor that runs in your browser. It checks your handler while you type, shows what Nucleus would set up for each player, lets you step through the code, and keeps the docs next to it.
when: You want to write or fix a handler right now and don't want to install anything.
You're new to handlers. The tour, the Lines list, the tips and Learn are there to help.
You're curious how a handler on the Hub works. Open it and run Check and Try it on it.
You're not at your own PC. Any modern browser will do, a phone included.
tools.not: One thing it can't do is start Nucleus Co-op, because browsers aren't allowed to start programs. For one-click testing in Nucleus, use VS Code, Notepad++ or `ncdev test`.

tools.title: VS Code
tools.what: The extension adds handler support to VS Code and VSCodium. Problems are underlined while you type and come with quick fixes. You also get suggestions, docs on hover and in a side panel, Try it, a debugger, and commands that package a handler, install it and start Nucleus Co-op with it.
when: You write handlers regularly. This is the setup with the most in it.
You already use VS Code for other things.
You want real breakpoints, in VS Code's own Run and Debug.
You use Copilot or another agent in VS Code. The extension hands it the Nucleus tools.
tools.videoLine: About a minute of problems, quick fixes, suggestions, parameter hints, the Docs panel and Try it.

tools.title: Notepad++
tools.what: A plugin for Notepad++, which came first when we asked handler authors what they write in. It underlines problems while you type, fixes them with Alt+Enter, suggests names and shows docs when you hover. Try it, the Hub, packaging and testing in Nucleus Co-op are in its menu.
when: You already write handlers in Notepad++ and see no reason to switch.
You like a light editor. Setup is one command, `ncdev setup notepad++`.
You want Install and Test in Nucleus Co-op in a menu.
tools.not: There's no debugger in the plugin. To step through a handler, use VS Code or the workbench.
tools.videoLine: Under a minute. The same checks, fixes, suggestions and docs, plus the plugin's menu.

tools.title: Other editors
tools.what: `ncdev lsp` is a language server for handlers. If your editor can talk to language servers, it gets the same problems, fixes, suggestions, hover docs, outline and formatting as VS Code. Editors with a debug client can also use `ncdev dap` for the debugger.
when: You use Neovim, Helix, Emacs, Kate, Sublime Text, a JetBrains IDE or Zed, and you're staying.
You don't mind adding a few lines to your editor's config.
Your editor isn't on the list but has a language-server client. The same server works there.
tools.not: Fair warning: only some of these setups have been tested so far. [The tools page](@site:tools/#in-your-editor) says which.

tools.title: ncdev (command line)
tools.what: `ncdev` is the command-line version of the tools, in one program. It checks and formats handlers, looks things up in the API, runs Try it and the debugger in a terminal, packages and installs handlers, starts Nucleus Co-op for a test, and searches the Hub. Notepad++ and the other editors run it in the background (`ncdev lsp`), and AI agents connect to it (`ncdev mcp`).
when: You want to check a whole folder of handlers in one go, maybe in a script or in CI.
You want a quick answer without opening an editor, like `ncdev api KillMutex`.
You're setting up Notepad++ or another editor. They need it.
You're connecting an AI agent to the tools.

get.label: Get the tools: the command line

tools.title: MCP server (AI agents)
tools.what: `ncdev mcp` is an MCP server. It lets an AI agent use the handler tools itself. The agent can look up what the API really has, check the handler it wrote, run Try it on it and ask what a line does. That beats an AI guessing at option names.
when: You write handlers with Claude Code, Codex, Copilot or some other agent that speaks MCP.
You'd like the handler to pass Check before the agent shows it to you.
tools.not: Chatbots without tools, like ChatGPT or Claude in a browser tab, can't use it. For those there's a prompt to paste on [Set up your AI](@site:ai/).
